title: Nehemiah 7:6–38
context: The record lists the returnees by leaders, by family, and by town. It closely parallels Ezra 2:1-35, but many numbers differ and several names are spelled differently or replaced; for example, Nehemiah 7:7 lists twelve leaders where Ezra 2:2 lists eleven, and Ezra 2:30 includes the children of Magbish, who are not listed here. Interpreters explain the differences in various ways, such as errors in copying numerals or lists drawn up at different stages; the notes name the differences without harmonizing them.

verses.text: These are the children of the province who went up out of the captivity of those who had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away, and who returned to Jerusalem and to Judah, everyone to his city,
verses.arminianNotes: These are the people of the province who returned from Babylon, each to his own town. Arminian readers see the list as a record of people who chose to leave exile and return to a ruined homeland.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the list God’s faithfulness in bringing his people back after the exile Nebuchadnezzar imposed. The verse matches Ezra 2:1 closely, opening the parallel record.

verses.text: who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verses.arminianNotes: The returnees came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, and others. Ezra 2:2 has eleven leaders where this verse has twelve, adding Nahamani, and Azariah, Raamiah, Mispereth, and Nehum stand where Ezra has Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mispar, and Rehum. Arminian readers see named leaders who chose to guide the return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Nehemiah named here is generally taken to be a different person from the book’s author, since this list concerns the first return. The leaders named first are Zerubbabel the governor and Jeshua the priest (Ezra 3:2).

verses.text: The children of Parosh: two thousand one hundred seventy-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Parosh heads the list with two thousand one hundred seventy-two, the same as Ezra 2:3. Arminian readers note that a son of Parosh later helped rebuild the wall (Nehemiah 3:25), so the family that returned also labored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the name Parosh appears again when the people seal the covenant (Nehemiah 10:14). One family line runs through return, rebuilding, and renewed commitment to God’s law.

verses.text: The children of Shephatiah: three hundred seventy-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Shephatiah’s family numbers three hundred seventy-two, matching Ezra 2:4. Arminian readers see in each line a real household that weighed the cost of the journey and decided to go.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that more of Shephatiah’s descendants arrived with Ezra decades afterward (Ezra 8:8). The repeated names show God gathering his people in more than one wave.

verses.text: The children of Arah: six hundred fifty-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Arah is credited with six hundred fifty-two here but seven hundred seventy-five in Ezra 2:5. Arminian readers leave this sizable gap unresolved, as the context note explains for the list as a whole.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Tobiah, Nehemiah’s opponent, married into a family descended from Arah (Nehemiah 6:18). A household counted among the returnees was also tied to the opposition.

verses.text: The children of Pahathmoab, of the children of Jeshua and Joab: two thousand eight hundred eighteen.
verses.arminianNotes: Pahathmoab, through Jeshua and Joab, has two thousand eight hundred eighteen, six more than Ezra 2:6. Arminian readers treat such small gaps as part of an honest record, not a threat to its trustworthiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Hasshub of this family repaired a section of the wall (Nehemiah 3:11). The name, meaning governor of Moab, may preserve an earlier office, though its origin is uncertain.

verses.text: The children of Elam: one thousand two hundred fifty-four.
verses.arminianNotes: Elam’s family numbers one thousand two hundred fifty-four, agreeing with Ezra 2:7. Arminian readers point out that the other Elam in verse 34 has exactly this figure as well, something the text leaves unexplained.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Shecaniah, from this family, later led the confession over foreign marriages (Ezra 10:2). Families on the list appear again in both failure and repentance.

verses.text: The children of Zattu: eight hundred forty-five.
verses.arminianNotes: Zattu has eight hundred forty-five, against nine hundred forty-five in Ezra 2:8. Arminian readers observe that here only the hundreds digit varies, one of several entries that differ in a single place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Zattu, like Parosh, is among the names that seal the covenant document (Nehemiah 10:14). Variations between the lists are named here without forcing them together.

verses.text: The children of Zaccai: seven hundred sixty.
verses.arminianNotes: Zaccai’s seven hundred sixty agrees with Ezra 2:9. Arminian readers see such matching lines as evidence that both books preserve the same body of returnees, despite variations elsewhere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the exact agreement here and in many entries shows the two books drawing on a common record. Where the figures agree, they agree to the last digit.

verses.text: The children of Binnui: six hundred forty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: Binnui has six hundred forty-eight. Ezra 2:10 names this family Bani and counts six hundred forty-two, so name and number both vary. Arminian readers simply record both readings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Binnui and Bani are similar in form, and interpreters discuss whether one family is meant. The notes name the variation without resolving it.

verses.text: The children of Bebai: six hundred twenty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: Bebai’s six hundred twenty-eight is five more than Ezra 2:11. Arminian readers remember that every figure stands for families with homes to rebuild and fields to plant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that a further group from Bebai traveled with Ezra (Ezra 8:11). The list records the first return, but the story of these families continues.

verses.text: The children of Azgad: two thousand three hundred twenty-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Azgad’s two thousand three hundred twenty-two far exceeds Ezra 2:12, which has one thousand two hundred twenty-two. Arminian readers see this as one of the largest gaps between the two lists.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Azgad also sent more members with Ezra (Ezra 8:12). A difference of eleven hundred is named, not explained away, and interpreters weigh possible reasons.

verses.text: The children of Adonikam: six hundred sixty-seven.
verses.arminianNotes: Adonikam has six hundred sixty-seven, one more than Ezra 2:13. Arminian readers see how easily a single unit could shift as lists were copied by hand over generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Adonikam’s later descendants joined Ezra’s company (Ezra 8:13). The variation is small, and interpreters suggest several possible causes, none of which the text itself confirms.

verses.text: The children of Bigvai: two thousand sixty-seven.
verses.arminianNotes: Bigvai has two thousand sixty-seven, eleven more than Ezra 2:14. Arminian readers note that Bigvai is also the name of a leader in verse 7, though the text does not link them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Bigvai’s family appears again in Ezra’s later caravan (Ezra 8:14). Whether leader and family share more than a name is left unstated.

verses.text: The children of Adin: six hundred fifty-five.
verses.arminianNotes: Adin has six hundred fifty-five, compared with four hundred fifty-four in Ezra 2:15. Arminian readers observe that two digits differ here, unlike the single-digit variations nearby.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Adin appears both in Ezra’s later company (Ezra 8:6) and among the covenant signers (Nehemiah 10:16), a family faithful across several stages of renewal.

verses.text: The children of Ater: of Hezekiah, ninety-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: Ater, through Hezekiah, numbers ninety-eight, as in Ezra 2:16. Arminian readers note that the phrase of Hezekiah marks out a particular branch within a larger family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ater and Hezekiah stand side by side again on the sealed covenant (Nehemiah 10:17). Whether this Hezekiah is the king is not stated in either place.

verses.text: The children of Hashum: three hundred twenty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: Hashum has three hundred twenty-eight, against two hundred twenty-three in Ezra 2:19. The order differs too: Hashum precedes Bezai here but follows Jorah in Ezra. Arminian readers record both differences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that members of Hashum’s family were among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:33). The list records families, not their later faithfulness.

verses.text: The children of Bezai: three hundred twenty-four.
verses.arminianNotes: Bezai has three hundred twenty-four, a single unit above Ezra 2:17. Arminian readers note that this family is listed in a slightly different position from the one it holds in Ezra’s order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bezai’s name is attached to the covenant document as well (Nehemiah 10:18). The family stands in the record of both the return and the renewal.

verses.text: The children of Hariph: one hundred twelve.
verses.arminianNotes: Hariph numbers one hundred twelve. Ezra 2:18 has Jorah with the same figure, so the name varies while the count holds steady. Arminian readers leave the relationship open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hariph is among the covenant signatories (Nehemiah 10:19). Interpreters discuss how Hariph and Jorah relate; the notes do not settle it.

verses.text: The children of Gibeon: ninety-five.
verses.arminianNotes: Gibeon has ninety-five. Ezra 2:20 reads Gibbar with the same number, so a place name stands here where Ezra has what looks like a family name. Arminian readers note the variation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the Gibeonites joined in repairing the wall (Nehemiah 3:7). From this verse onward, the list identifies most groups by their towns.

verses.text: The men of Bethlehem and Netophah: one hundred eighty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: Bethlehem and Netophah together number one hundred eighty-eight. Ezra 2:21-22 lists them separately as one hundred twenty-three and fifty-six, a combined one hundred seventy-nine. Arminian readers record the gap.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bethlehem was David’s town and that men of Netophah were among David’s mighty men (2 Samuel 23:28-29). The different totals are named without resolution.

verses.text: The men of Anathoth: one hundred twenty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Anathoth: one hundred twenty-eight, matching Ezra 2:23. Arminian readers note that Anathoth was Jeremiah’s hometown (Jeremiah 1:1), where he bought a field as a sign of future return (Jeremiah 32:6-15).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the return of Anathoth’s men as a quiet fulfillment of Jeremiah’s hope. The prophet’s purchase pointed to a day when fields would again be bought in the land.

verses.text: The men of Beth Azmaveth: forty-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Beth Azmaveth sends forty-two. Ezra 2:24 calls the town simply Azmaveth, with the same figure, a minor variation in the place name. Arminian readers see villagers reclaiming their homes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Azmaveth reappears among the villages of the singers (Nehemiah 12:29). Its exact location is uncertain, though it is generally placed in Benjamin.

verses.text: The men of Kiriath Jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth: seven hundred forty-three.
verses.arminianNotes: Kiriath Jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth together send seven hundred forty-three. Ezra 2:25 spells the first town Kiriath Arim, with the same total. Arminian readers see three towns returning as one group.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these were among the Gibeonite towns of Joshua 9:17, and that Kiriath Jearim sheltered the ark for many years (1 Samuel 7:1-2). Old associations return with the people.

verses.text: The men of Ramah and Geba: six hundred twenty-one.
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Ramah and Geba: six hundred twenty-one, matching Ezra 2:26. Arminian readers note that Ramah was Samuel’s home (1 Samuel 7:17), a reminder of Israel’s earlier history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that these towns lay in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. The return restores communities in the region that had once formed the border between Judah and Israel.

verses.text: The men of Michmas: one hundred twenty-two.
verses.arminianNotes: Michmas sends one hundred twenty-two, matching Ezra 2:27. Arminian readers recall that Michmash was the site of Jonathan’s daring attack on the Philistines (1 Samuel 14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a place once known for a battle receiving families back from exile. The list quietly ties the restored community to Israel’s earlier history.

verses.text: The men of Bethel and Ai: one hundred twenty-three.
verses.arminianNotes: Bethel and Ai send one hundred twenty-three, a hundred fewer than Ezra 2:28. Arminian readers recall that Abram built an altar between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 12:8), a place of early worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bethel later became the site of Jeroboam’s calf shrine (1 Kings 12:29). Its people now return to a land being restored to the worship of the LORD in Jerusalem.

verses.text: The men of the other Nebo: fifty-two.
verses.arminianNotes: The other Nebo sends fifty-two. Ezra 2:29 says simply Nebo, with the same figure, and Ezra 2:30 then adds Magbish, one hundred fifty-six, an entry with no counterpart here. Arminian readers record the omission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the word other may distinguish this Nebo from a better-known place of the same name, though the identification is uncertain. The absence of Magbish is named without explanation.

verses.text: The children of the other Elam: one thousand two hundred fifty-four.
verses.arminianNotes: The other Elam’s figure agrees with Ezra 2:31. Arminian readers observe that this matches the first Elam of verse 12 exactly, a coincidence the list does not address.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that interpreters discuss whether the identical figures reflect two families or some other explanation. The text records the number and moves on.

verses.text: The children of Harim: three hundred twenty.
verses.arminianNotes: Harim’s lay family numbers three hundred twenty, as in Ezra 2:32. Arminian readers note that a priestly Harim appears in verse 42 with more than three times as many members.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this lay family is distinct from the priestly house of the same name. Names recur in the list, and the setting tells which group is meant.

verses.text: The children of Jericho: three hundred forty-five.
verses.arminianNotes: Jericho sends three hundred forty-five, agreeing with Ezra 2:34. In Ezra, however, Lod comes first and Jericho second, so the sequence is reversed here. Arminian readers note the change of order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers recall that Jericho’s men built next to the priests who rebuilt the Sheep Gate (Nehemiah 3:1-2). The city once rebuilt under Joshua’s curse (1 Kings 16:34) now shelters faithful returnees.

verses.text: The children of Lod, Hadid, and Ono: seven hundred twenty-one.
verses.arminianNotes: Lod, Hadid, and Ono send seven hundred twenty-one, four fewer than Ezra 2:33. Arminian readers see towns on the western edge of the province rejoining the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ono is the plain where Nehemiah’s enemies tried to lure him (Nehemiah 6:2). These towns lay toward the coastal plain, west of Jerusalem.

verses.text: The children of Senaah: three thousand nine hundred thirty.
verses.arminianNotes: Senaah has three thousand nine hundred thirty, three hundred more than Ezra 2:35. Arminian readers observe that in both lists this is the largest single group of lay returnees.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the sons of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate (Nehemiah 3:3), possibly the same group. The location and nature of Senaah are uncertain.
